cases.title: Multan Sewage Plant, Suraj Miani: Crops and Trees Destroyed by Contractor
cases.place: Akbar Pur village, Suraj Miani, Multan, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Suraj Miani, on the north side of Multan; the plant site lies off Suraj Miani Road towards the Chenab River (approximate)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loans 2060/2061-PAK of US$90 million for the Southern Punjab Basic Urban Services Project, approved on 18 December 2003, which financed the Multan wastewater treatment plant at Akbar Pur, Suraj Miani (ADB Special Project Facilitator, 2009).

cases.conditions: An ADB-financed urban services loan covering 21 towns in Southern Punjab; in Multan it paid for a wastewater treatment plant on farmland acquired under Pakistan's Land Acquisition Act and a December 2007 resettlement plan (ADB Special Project Facilitator review and assessment report, 2009).
cases.community: The complainants were 55 affected people, mostly small landowners growing wheat, barley, potatoes, tomatoes, sugarcane and fruit trees (ADB Special Project Facilitator). They said that the plant's contractor entered their fields without notice (they were asking ADB for help against it from late December 2008) and destroyed standing crops, old mango trees and date palms, damaged some houses, tube wells and irrigation channels, and, according to two complainants, a mosque. Women farm labourers lost their work; some stayed at home and others took jobs as household helpers in Multan. The facilitator's office found that a number of complainants had suffered for months, that some were selling assets to survive and that others were in debt to traders who had paid in advance for the destroyed harvest. Everyone agreed the first compensation rate of PRs 500,000 per acre was too low, and it was raised to PRs 1.5 million per acre; complainants who knew of the new rate still rejected it (ADB Special Project Facilitator, 2009).
cases.outcome: At ADB's request, construction at the plant stopped on 9 January 2009 and ADB suspended the subproject while it reviewed resettlement and environmental safeguards. The Special Project Facilitator declared the complaint eligible on 25 May 2009, proposed facilitated talks and suggested that completing Multan's sewage system be moved into a later Punjab Cities Improvement Project. The facilitator's final report (23 May 2012) has not been made public (ADB Accountability Mechanism).

cases.title: Lahore North 500 kV Grid Station: Farmland of 120 Households Acquired
cases.place: Sheikhupura–Muridke Road near Khairpur Malian and Seekham villages, Lahore Division, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Sheikhupura–Muridke Road, along which the grid station was built (approximate; exact site not given in the sources)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Tranche 3 of the Second Power Transmission Enhancement Investment Program (Loan 3677, Grant 0578), approved on 28 June 2018, which financed a 500 kV substation in Lahore North among other works (ADB Special Project Facilitator final report, 2025).

cases.conditions: An ADB multitranche loan to Pakistan's National Transmission and Dispatch Company (NTDC) for substations, 194 km of new lines and a battery storage pilot, classed category A for involuntary resettlement (ADB Special Project Facilitator, 2025).
cases.community: The land chosen for the 500 kV grid station belonged to 120 households. Their representatives told ADB that NTDC had moved the site onto fertile farmland that was the families' only source of income, and that homes, dairy and fish farms and an ancestral graveyard would be removed; 42 of the households handed in a written complaint during ADB's 8 July 2019 mission. NTDC refused to move the station. After ADB-facilitated talks it cut the plot by nearly 32 acres from a planned 200 acres, and on 30 June 2021 returned (denotified) 13.6 acres to owners; the rest was acquired and the substation built on it. The complainants said NTDC's compensation for land fell short of ADB's replacement-cost rule and filed a petition in the Lahore High Court (ADB Special Project Facilitator, 2025).
cases.outcome: A memorandum of understanding signed on 2 February 2021 gave a 100-foot access road without boundary walls, a drain to stop flooding of nearby fields, no transmission lines over returned land and job referrals; the complainants withdrew their High Court petition in 2022. None of the three CVs they submitted met the contractors' technical requirements. ADB's facilitator closed the complaint in July 2025, rejecting a further claim that new footpaths blocked access to fields (ADB Special Project Facilitator, 2025).

cases.title: Jalalpur Canal: 8,558 Acres Acquired and Villages Cut Off
cases.place: Jalalpur canal from Rasul Barrage through Pind Dadan Khan (Jhelum district) to Khushab, Punjab, Pakistan
cases.point: Pind Dadan Khan, the tehsil crossed by the main canal where most complaints arose (approximate)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Loan 3599-PAK of US$274.63 million for the Jalalpur Irrigation Project, approved on 24 November 2017, effective 31 May 2018, closing extended to 31 December 2027 (ADB project page).

cases.conditions: An ADB loan for a new non-perennial canal system and flood carrier channels to irrigate 79,750 hectares in Jhelum and Khushab districts, classed category A for involuntary resettlement, with land taken under land acquisition and resettlement plans (ADB project page; ADB complaint closing reports).
cases.community: The external monitor's report to ADB for July–December 2025 records 8,558 acres acquired for the canal and a staff colony, with 22 houses (22 households to be relocated), 236 livestock sheds and tube-well fixtures, 9,524 trees, 93 fruit plants and two public schools affected, and 143,871 displaced persons listed, 763 of them classed as vulnerable in one table and 819 in another. Some had not been paid because owners had died, lived elsewhere, had mutation (land-record) problems or court cases, or found the sums too small to collect. The same report records that during the 2025 monsoon land between the hills and the right bank of the main canal flooded, damaging a road, some houses, land and other structures, and that the district administration opened drainage through a flood-channel culvert; it notes earlier complaints of standing water upstream of that flood-channel structure at the main canal, but does not say the canal caused the flooding (external social monitoring report, 2026). In Daulatpur village, Pind Dadan Khan (about 4,000 people), resident Noor Muhammad told Lok Sujag that about 222 acres of the village's land had become unusable because of the canal, and the planned rainwater drain was to take more than 120 acres of its farmland (Lok Sujag, 2022). Residents of Wara Buland Khan told ADB in January 2026 that the canal blocked old drainage paths, that recent rains had submerged houses, and that the canal split the village from its fields and graveyard with no bridge (complaint to ADB). Between 2020 and 2026 at least 13 complaints about land, alignment, drainage and compensation reached ADB's Accountability Mechanism.
cases.outcome: Most complaints were sent back to the project's grievance process. In two that ADB reported on, the project shifted a flood channel's alignment and cut the right-of-way to 65 feet (from 155 feet in one case), and the complainants withdrew (ADB closing reports, 2024–2025). Two complaints were found eligible for ADB problem-solving in July 2025 and March 2026 and were still under review. By August 2026 the canal had been put into trial operation; Sindh province opposes it over its share of Indus water (Dawn, 2026).

cases.title: Naga, Cebu Coal Plant: Coal Dust, Ash and a Stop Order
cases.place: Barangay Colon, Naga City, Cebu, Philippines
cases.point: Barangay Colon, Naga City, site of the KEPCO-SPC coal plant (approximate)

lenders.name: Asian Development Bank
lenders.role: Direct loan of up to US$120 million to KEPCO/SPC Power Corporation, approved 11 December 2009 and effective 4 March 2010; US$86 million had been disbursed by late 2011 (ADB Compliance Review Panel, 2012).

lenders.name: Export-Import Bank of Korea
lenders.role: Co-lender; the project was ADB's first collaboration with the Korean Export-Import Bank (ADB Compliance Review Panel, 2012).

cases.conditions: A private-sector loan, without government guarantee, for a 200 MW coal plant with circulating fluidized bed boilers, built on the ash pond area of the existing Naga power plant (ADB Compliance Review Panel, 2012).

companies.name: KEPCO SPC Power Corporation
companies.role: Plant owner and borrower; 60% owned by Korea Electric Power Corporation Philippine Holdings and 40% by SPC Power Corporation

cases.community: Building the plant and its transmission link displaced 22 families; 17 were moved in 2008 onto land reclaimed with old coal ash that had no environmental permits, topsoil cover or septic tanks (ADB Compliance Review Panel, 2012). A regional trial court issued a temporary environmental protection order on 17 August 2010 banning the Naga plants from moving and dumping ash outside their sites, extended to KEPCO-SPC on 15 March 2011 (ADB Compliance Review Panel). Residents said ash was dumped in the hills of Colon in February 2011, which the company denied (Philippine Daily Inquirer). In March 2011 Cebu Governor Gwen Garcia closed the plant's open coal stockyard for several weeks after coal dust reached homes (Philippine Daily Inquirer). On 13 November 2012 Naga Mayor Valdemar Chiong ordered coal loading and unloading stopped after residents complained that black dust from the coal yard had reached their houses; households said it soiled furniture and clothes and that children and elderly people fell ill with coughs and colds. KEPCO-SPC admitted the dust came from raw coal delivered to the plant (The Freeman; Philippine Daily Inquirer).
cases.outcome: ADB's Compliance Review Panel found that ADB had not done rigorous due diligence on ash management and air dispersion, had not identified that the resettlement site was an old ash dump, and had not addressed health concerns; it said the potential for harm to health and environment existed but it was too early to establish it with certainty, and that health records suggested air emissions in the area were likely affecting residents. The Board approved its recommendations, including ash-utilisation studies and management plans for old ash sites, on 11 April 2012. The 2012 stop order was lifted on 15 November 2012 after the company promised lower stockpiles, net covers over the coal yard and street clean-up teams (ADB; Philstar).

cases.confidence_note: No study has proved illness caused by this plant: the Compliance Review Panel said harm was possible but too early to establish with certainty, and the area also had an older coal plant and a cement plant. The dust episodes are recorded through official closure and stop orders and the company's own admission in 2012; the 2011 ash-dumping report rests on residents and was denied by the company. The 2008 relocation onto ash land came before ADB began due diligence in early 2009 and approved the loan in December 2009, but ADB's review of that resettlement plan was among the failures the Panel found. The Inquirer pages carry no printed date.
